items.prompt: What is a glacier made of?

options.label: Natural ice that is constantly moving under its own weight
options.feedback: Correct. A glacier is a persistent body of natural ice that flows and deforms under its own weight.

options.label: Frozen seawater that forms on the ocean surface
options.feedback: That describes sea ice, not a glacier. Glaciers originate only on land.

options.label: Compacted snow that stays still all year
options.feedback: A glacier is constantly moving, not still. Snow that stays put is just a snowfield.

options.label: Rock made of frozen minerals
options.feedback: Glaciers are ice, not rock. Although ice is sometimes called a rock, the material is frozen water.

items.ok_line: A glacier is moving natural ice.
items.ko_line: Sea ice is different from glacier ice.
items.exp_text: A glacier is a persistent body of natural ice that constantly moves under its own weight. It forms on land, not on water, and is distinct from the much thinner sea ice and lake ice that freeze on the surface of bodies of water.

options.label: In the middle of the ocean
options.feedback: Glaciers do not form on the ocean. They originate only on land, even though some may later flow into water.

options.label: On land, often in a bowl-shaped depression between mountains
options.feedback: Correct. A glacier usually starts in a cirque, an armchair-shaped depression that collects snow.

options.label: At the bottom of a lake
options.feedback: Lake ice forms on the surface of freezing lakes, but that is not a glacier. Glaciers need land to start.

options.label: On a flat plain with no mountains
options.feedback: While ice sheets can cover flat land, a glacier typically originates from a cirque in mountainous terrain.

items.exp_text: A glacier usually originates from a cirque, a bowl- or armchair-shaped depression between mountains. Snow accumulates there, compresses, and eventually overflows as glacial ice. It forms only on land.

items.prompt: What is the name for the zone of a glacier where there is a net loss of mass?

options.label: Accumulation zone
options.feedback: That is the opposite. The accumulation zone is where snow gain exceeds loss, not where there is a net loss.

options.label: Equilibrium line
options.feedback: The equilibrium line is the boundary between gain and loss, not the zone itself where loss dominates.

options.label: Ablation zone
options.feedback: Correct. The ablation zone is the region where the glacier loses more mass than it gains.

options.label: Glacier head
options.feedback: The glacier head is simply the starting point of the glacier, not a zone of net mass loss.

items.ok_line: Loss happens in the ablation zone.
items.ko_line: Accumulation is gain, ablation is loss.
items.exp_text: The ablation zone is the lower part of a glacier where melting and other losses exceed new snow. In contrast, the accumulation zone is where new snow adds more than is lost, and the equilibrium line separates the two.

items.prompt: What happens to snow as it turns into glacial ice?

options.label: It becomes lighter and full of air
options.feedback: The opposite is true. Glacial ice has fewer trapped air bubbles because pressure squeezes the air out.

options.label: It melts completely and refreezes as solid water
options.feedback: While melting can occur in temperate glaciers, the main process is compaction and fusion of snow grains, not complete melting.

options.label: It stays as loose, granular snow
options.feedback: Granular snow is called névé, which is an intermediate stage, not the final glacial ice.

options.label: It compresses, expels air, and becomes denser ice
options.feedback: Correct. Snow turns into névé, then firn, and finally glacial ice as pressure packs the grains and squeezes out air.

items.ok_line: Pressure turns snow into dense ice.
items.ko_line: Compaction, not melting, forms glacial ice.
items.exp_text: Snow accumulates, refreezes, and turns into granular névé. Further crushing expels air, turning it into firn and eventually glacial ice, which is denser and has fewer air bubbles than freshly frozen water.

options.label: A glacial body larger than 50,000 square kilometres
options.feedback: Correct. Ice sheets, also called continental glaciers, are larger than 50,000 km² and cover vast areas.

options.label: A thin layer of ice on a lake
options.feedback: Lake ice is not a glacier at all, and it is much smaller than an ice sheet.

options.label: A glacier that fills a mountain valley
options.feedback: That is a valley glacier, not an ice sheet. Ice sheets are much larger and cover entire regions.

options.label: A fast-moving section of a glacier
options.feedback: Fast-moving sections are called ice streams, not ice sheets. Ice sheets move slowly overall.

items.ok_line: Ice sheets are huge glacial bodies.
items.exp_text: An ice sheet, or continental glacier, is a glacial body larger than 50,000 square kilometres. Only two exist today, covering most of Antarctica and Greenland. Smaller glacial bodies on mountains are ice caps or ice fields.

items.prompt: What happens when a tidewater glacier reaches the sea?

options.label: It stops moving entirely
options.feedback: Tidewater glaciers keep flowing into the sea; they do not stop at the shoreline.

options.label: Pieces break off and form icebergs
options.feedback: Correct. This process is called calving, and the broken pieces become icebergs.

options.label: It melts completely before touching the water
options.feedback: Tidewater glaciers do reach the water; that is what makes them tidewater glaciers. They do not melt entirely at the coast.

options.label: It turns into sea ice
options.feedback: Sea ice forms from freezing ocean water, not from glacier ice. Calved ice floats as icebergs but is not sea ice.

items.ok_line: Glaciers calve icebergs at the sea.
items.ko_line: Calved ice is glacier ice, not sea ice.
items.exp_text: Tidewater glaciers terminate in the sea. As the ice reaches the water, pieces break off—this is called calving—and form icebergs. Most tidewater glaciers calve above sea level, causing a big splash as the ice hits the water.

options.label: A type of glacial valley
options.feedback: Nunataks are not valleys. They are rock peaks that stick up through the ice.

options.label: A fast-moving ice stream
options.feedback: Ice streams are different features. Nunataks are exposed rocky summits, not moving ice.

options.label: A mountain peak that protrudes above an ice sheet
options.feedback: Correct. Nunataks are the only parts of the underlying topography that stick out from an ice sheet's surface.

options.label: A deep crevasse in the ice
options.feedback: Crevasses are cracks in the ice, not rocky peaks. Nunataks are solid rock.

items.exp_text: A nunatak is a mountain peak or ridge that protrudes above the surface of an ice sheet or glacier. Ice sheets are so thick they hide the underlying land, except where such rocky summits break through.

items.prompt: What color does a large body of glacial ice appear?

options.label: White
options.feedback: White ice comes from trapped air bubbles, but glacial ice has few bubbles, so it is not white.

options.label: Clear
options.feedback: Glacial ice is not fully clear; it has a blue tint due to how water molecules absorb light.

options.label: Green
options.feedback: Green is not the natural color of glacial ice. The blue comes from water's absorption of other colors.

options.label: Blue
options.feedback: Correct. Water molecules absorb other colors more efficiently than blue, and glacial ice has few air bubbles, so it appears blue.

items.ko_line: Air bubbles make ice white, not blue.
items.exp_text: Glacial ice appears blue because water molecules absorb red and other colors more than blue. Also, the pressure of the ice squeezes out air bubbles, which would otherwise scatter light and make the ice look white.

items.prompt: What is the equilibrium line on a glacier?

options.label: The contour where snow gain equals ice loss
options.feedback: Correct. The equilibrium line separates the accumulation zone from the ablation zone where gains and losses balance.

options.label: The line where the glacier meets the ocean
options.feedback: That is the terminus or snout of a tidewater glacier, not the equilibrium line.

options.label: The topmost edge of the glacier
options.feedback: The top is the glacier head, not the equilibrium line. The equilibrium line is inside the glacier.

options.label: The boundary between ice and rock underneath
options.feedback: The base of the glacier is the bed, not the equilibrium line. The equilibrium line is on the surface.

items.ok_line: Gain equals loss at this line.
items.ko_line: The equilibrium line is internal, not a boundary.
items.exp_text: The equilibrium line is the contour on a glacier where the amount of new snow gained equals the amount lost through melting and other processes. Above it is the accumulation zone; below it is the ablation zone.

options.label: A thick layer of ice on a frozen lake
options.feedback: Lake ice is not part of a glacier, and ice shelves are extensions of ice sheets into water, not lake ice.

options.label: A portion of an ice sheet that extends into water
options.feedback: Correct. Ice shelves are thin, flat extensions of ice sheets or caps that float on the sea.

options.label: A narrow, fast-moving stream of ice
options.feedback: That is an ice stream, not an ice shelf. Ice streams are fast-moving, but they are not the floating extensions.

options.label: A glacier that terminates on land
options.feedback: An ice shelf specifically extends into water. A land-terminating glacier does not form an ice shelf.

items.ko_line: Ice streams move fast; shelves float.
items.exp_text: An ice shelf is a portion of an ice sheet or ice cap that extends out into a body of water. It tends to be thin, with limited slopes and slow movement, unlike the faster ice streams that drain ice sheets.
